title: Code review when agents write the code: reviewing intent, not lines
summary: Ada and Alan take code review apart into the four jobs it always bundled — teaching, norms, gatekeeping, catching bugs — then use the Harvard Jellyfish study's two-channel model (more code to read versus code that is harder to check) to explain why agent output piles up at review, and what intent review, risk routing, independent checks and provenance can and cannot replace.

topics: deep dive: code review when agents write the code
concepts_taught: code review as four bundled jobs (teaching the author, maintaining norms, gatekeeping/ownership, accident prevention) that an agent author breaks differently: norms move to linters and instructions, ownership stays a human approval, teaching moves into the rules file, and bug-catching grows from the smallest job to the largest

the two channels by which coding agents load review (Chen & Stratton): a productivity channel that is a queue and can be relieved by moving labor into review, and a bug-rate channel that raises scrutiny per unit of code and cuts good output — distinguished in the data by change requests nearly doubling at unchanged pull-request size

intent review with risk routing and independent checks: approval rules that know a change's kind, executable acceptance gates the authoring agent cannot see (because a visible test is a target — building to the test), and provenance for what inspection of an artifact can never guarantee

lore.note: Ada staked out that with agent authors the most valuable artifact in a pull request is a statement of intent written before the code, not generated after it — Fagan's 'reader' role coming back. Alan half-agreed, holding that he often only learns what he wants by watching the agent get it wrong, and they left open whether automating review automates away the apprenticeship that produces reviewers.

listener_note: spend 3-4 minutes on each of the selected dives and 2 minutes on the thinking inertia paper and 2 minutes on models provably hiding arbitrary capabilities. Spend at least a minute on the Harvard physicist's 36 manuscripts in 3 months. Episode can be up to 23 minutes today if needed
